claims.text: The as-deposited protective coating has a dual-phase microstructure containing both FCC and BCC grains.
The coating has nano- to sub-micron grain sizes.
A controlled heat treatment can modify the FCC/BCC phase volume fractions while leaving alloy composition unchanged.
Adjusting cooling rates can increase the BCC phase fraction.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries create localized lattice distortions.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries generate residual or internal stress fields.
Stress fields associated with FCC/BCC lattice mismatch impede dislocation movement and climb.
FCC/BCC interfaces impede grain-boundary sliding under sustained loading.
High-entropy alloys exhibit inherently sluggish diffusion.
Sluggish diffusion reduces the atomic rearrangement needed for creep deformation.
Interface barriers and diffusion limitation together stabilize the coating against progressive plastic deformation.
Increasing the BCC phase fraction produces more, or more effective, FCC/BCC interfaces.
A coating with an increased BCC fraction will have a lower steady-state creep rate than the as-deposited baseline under identical loading conditions.
The proposed behavior applies at approximately 0.5–0.7 times the melting temperature, where dislocation motion and limited diffusion both operate.
The proposed mechanism applies at stresses sufficient to activate creep but below those causing extensive plastic flow or catastrophic failure.
At temperatures approaching 0.8 times the melting temperature, diffusion or other deformation mechanisms may dominate and diminish interface effects.
At extremely high stress, other deformation mechanisms may dominate and limit the hypothesis's applicability.
Failure to observe a statistically significant creep-rate reduction after increasing the BCC fraction would reject the proposed FCC/BCC-interface mechanism.
